The Relationship Trump Misunderstood:
For three decades, China and emerging markets effectively exported disinflation to the developed world. They produced goods at a fraction of Western costs and shipped them to consumers in the US and Europe. The result: lower prices and higher purchasing power
The West got cheaper TVs, phones, clothes, furniture and industrial goods. China got manufacturing jobs, export growth and rising incomes. It wasn't a one-way relationship. Both sides benefited
As exports surged, China accumulated enormous foreign exchange reserves. Every dollar earned from exports added to a growing pool of savings that had to be invested somewhere
Those reserves served two purposes: protect the yuan from volatility and build strategic national wealth. China used them to buy foreign assets, resources, companies and financial securities around the world
A large portion of those reserves found their way into US Treasuries. China became one of the largest lenders to the US government, recycling export earnings back into America's financial system
This mattered because sustained Treasury demand helped keep long-term US interest rates lower than they otherwise would have been. Cheap imports lowered inflation. Treasury purchases lowered financing costs
In effect, China was helping on two fronts: suppressing goods inflation through low-cost manufacturing and supporting bond markets through reserve recycling. 
Trump focused heavily on one side of the equation: the trade deficit. From that perspective, China was exporting too much and manufacturing jobs were leaving America. This became the basis for tariffs and trade confrontation.
But the other side received less attention. Those same imports were keeping prices low for US consumers. Many products became affordable precisely because they were manufactured in lower-cost economies
The relationship also extended to capital markets. China's reserve accumulation created a steady source of demand for US government bonds, helping support the broader financial system
Today that world is changing. China is no longer a low-income economy desperate for export growth. Wages have risen, technology has improved and its economic influence is far greater than it was 20 years ago
The old model of unlimited cheap labour, ever-rising globalization and automatic reserve recycling is fading. Both countries increasingly view the relationship through a strategic lens rather than purely an economic one
As supply chains fragment and tariffs rise, the US may face more inflation from its own policy choices. Producing goods domestically or through alternative supply chains is often more resilient, but rarely cheaper
At the same time, if foreign demand for Treasuries becomes less predictable, bond investors may demand higher yields to absorb increasing government debt. Higher yields mean higher financing costs across the economy
The next decade may look very different from the last three. Less globalization, more strategic competition, potentially higher inflation and structurally higher interest rates. Markets are still figuring out what that world looks like
Bottom line: The US-China relationship wasn't simply buyer vs seller. It was a system where goods, capital and inflation dynamics were deeply intertwined. Breaking that system may create consequences on both sides.

reports.text:
Patel Retail Limited Q1 FY27 Concall Highlights

Business Overview
Patel Retail Limited is an integrated food processing and value retail player operating through its Patel R-Mart store network, an expanding portfolio of private label brands (such as Indian Chaska), and an established distribution network focused on everyday household requirements.

Financial & Operational Performance Q1 FY27
• Total Income stood at ₹310.24 Cr, up 69.35% YoY
• EBITDA stood at ₹19.68 Cr, up 23.92% YoY
• PAT stood at ₹9.52 Cr, up 37.43% YoY
• EPS stood at ₹2.85 for the quarter
• EBITDA margin reported at 6.3% in Q1 impacted by 133–233 bps due to higher raw material intensity, product mix (manufacturing/exports), and raw material price volatility

Store Expansion & Retail Metrics:
• Added 2 new stores during Q1 FY27 (Rasayani and Babgaon) and reached 53 stores post-quarter with an opening in Uran, Raigad.
• Total retail selling area expanded to ~2.42 lakh sq. ft.
• Average store size ranges between 5,000 to 6,000 sq. ft., with initial payback period of ~24 months per store
• Average monthly sales per store stand between ₹80 lakh to ₹1 Cr (averaging ~₹20,000 per sq. ft. sales in Q1FY27)
• Average customer order ticket size ranges from ₹500 to ₹1,000
• Planning 8 to 10 additional store openings in FY27 utilizing cluster-based expansion

Private Labels, Revenue Mix & Brand Expansion
• Flagship brand Indian Chaska expanded into Madhya Pradesh, extending presence across 8 states and 1 union territory
• Private label sales contributed 17.55% of overall retail revenue, 37% of export sales, and 45% of domestic sales
• Business segment breakdown: ~40% contributed by exports and ~60% by retail/manufacturing

OMCs, AUTO STOCKS: GOVT EXPLORES RETURN OF E10 PETROL AS PREMIUM FUEL OPTION

⛽ Petroleum Ministry is exploring bringing back E10 petrol, amid consumer concerns over E20 fuel’s impact on older vehicles and mileage.

🏭 Government is discussing the proposal with state-run OMCs Indian Oil, BPCL and HPCL, with branded 95-octane petrol being considered for an E10 formulation.

💰 Octane 95 currently costs around ₹110–115/litre vs ₹102/litre for regular petrol in Delhi, making the proposed E10 option a premium offering.

📈 Octane 95 now accounts for around 15% of OMC petrol sales vs just 4% in March, as consumers increasingly shift toward premium fuels.

⚠️ Discussions are still at an initial stage and no final decision has been taken.

🟢 Impact: Positive for OMCs & older-vehicle owners — premium E10 could provide additional consumer choice while potentially supporting higher-value fuel sales.

reports.text:
BSE, BROKING STOCKS: NSE DERIVATIVES TURNOVER SLUMPS AS STRICTER RULES HIT TRADING ACTIVITY

📉 NSE options premium turnover fell to around ₹67,000 Cr on Tuesday’s monthly expiry — lowest since December / since the shift to Tuesday expiry, highlighting a sharp slowdown in derivatives activity. 

⚠️ Key pressure comes from higher trading costs, tighter RBI funding/bank-guarantee norms for proprietary traders and reduced weekly expiries. 

📊 The new Closing Auction Session (CAS) is also changing expiry-day strategies and has kept participation relatively muted as traders adjust to the new mechanism. 

🔻 BSE options average daily turnover in August was already down ~12% vs July, showing the slowdown isn't limited to NSE. 

🔴 Impact: Negative for BSE & broking stocks — sustained lower F&O volumes can hurt transaction-fee income for exchanges and trading/brokerage revenues for brokers.

BlueStone vs PNGS Reva: The Tech Unicorn vs the 194-Year Legacy — Two Very Different Bets on India's Jewellery Boom

Both companies just posted extraordinary Q1 FY27 numbers. Both are riding the same structural shift — Indian consumers moving away from unorganized gold buying toward certified, design-led jewellery. 

But BlueStone and PNGS Reva are betting on completely opposite playbooks to win that shift. Let me walk you through both.

Two very different starting points

-->BlueStone Jewellery and Lifestyle — a digital-first, omni-channel consumer tech platform that happens to sell jewellery. Target audience: 25-45 year olds, daily wear and modern occasion pieces.

-->PNGS Reva Diamond Jewellery — leverages the 194-year legacy of P. N. Gadgil & Sons, running a hybrid Shop-in-Shop and Company-Owned model. Target audience: mass-affluent to premium buyers, focused on bridal and gifting occasions.

One built its brand from scratch through technology. The other borrowed nearly two centuries of trust from its parent group.

The headline scoreboard

-->Store count: BlueStone at 352 stores across 139 cities (852,000 sq ft) versus PNGS Reva's much leaner 37 stores (34 Shop-in-Shop + 3 Company-Owned) across 25 cities.

-->Revenue: BlueStone ₹733.2 Cr, up 48.8% YoY, versus PNGS Reva ₹118.0 Cr, up a staggering 119.5% YoY. BlueStone is more than 6x the scale, but Reva is growing more than twice as fast off its smaller base.

-->Same-Store Sales Growth: BlueStone at 39.0% YoY, broad-based across its network, versus PNGS Reva at ~50.0% YoY in its SIS stores specifically — both genuinely exceptional numbers by retail standards.

Where the margin story flips completely

-->Gross Margin: BlueStone at 40.7% (contribution margin 36.1%) versus PNGS Reva at 35.5%, up sharply from 31.4% a year ago.

-->Operating EBITDA: BlueStone's Pre-Ind AS EBITDA came to ₹54.8 Cr at a 7.5% margin (reported EBITDA ₹110.2 Cr at 15.0%). PNGS Reva posted ₹33.9 Cr at a 28.8% margin — nearly double BlueStone's reported rate, on a fraction of the revenue.

-->PAT: BlueStone's adjusted PAT was ₹13.8 Cr at a thin 1.9% margin. PNGS Reva delivered ₹27.2 Cr at a 23.1% margin — actually more absolute profit than BlueStone, despite doing roughly one-sixth the revenue.

That gap is the whole story of this comparison — BlueStone is optimizing for scale and market share today, while PNGS Reva is already running at retail-sector-leading profitability.

Why the margins look so different — it comes down to how each company spends money to grow

-->BlueStone's ticket size: Average Order Value of ₹78,081, up 40.7% YoY. Repeat revenue makes up 59.7% of sales (up 900 bps YoY), from a base of 9.84 lakh lifetime customers.

-->PNGS Reva's ticket size: Average Order Value of ₹1,00,232, up 8.2% YoY — a meaningfully higher average transaction, reflecting its more premium, bridal-and-gifting-skewed customer base.

-->BlueStone's manufacturing strategy: 95%+ in-house manufacturing with rapid 3D prototyping — this protects design IP from leaking to competitors and gives them pricing control, but also means they carry the capital intensity of running their own factories.

-->PNGS Reva's sourcing advantage: leans on the vendor network built over 194 years by the P. N. Gadgil group — letting them source efficiently without owning manufacturing infrastructure themselves.

-->Gold hedging: BlueStone runs a 50% gold hedging policy through Gold Metal Loans, a price-point-driven model built for volume. 

PNGS Reva does natural periodic procurement, and importantly, raw gold is a smaller component of their overall product value (~40%) since diamonds and making charges make up over 60% of price — a structurally different cost exposure to gold price swings.

Product mix — both are dodging the same landmine differently

-->BlueStone: 57.0% studded jewellery share, spanning 10,000+ unique designs across 14KT and 18KT gold, with dedicated Men's and Kids' lines. 

Price points run from ₹25,000-35,000 for daily wear up to ₹35,000-50,000 for occasion wear, with 6,000+ designs available under ₹60,000 — a genuinely accessible price ladder.

-->PNGS Reva: 100% natural diamond studded focus, split across Diamond Rings (27%), Mangalsutras (29%), Earrings (21%), and Necklaces & Bangles. 

Price points span much wider — from ₹15,000-35,000 entry level, up through ₹35,000-1.50 Lakh core everyday, all the way to ₹1.50 Lakh-25 Lakh+ for premium and bridal pieces.

-->Lab-Grown Diamond risk — both companies are genuinely insulated here. BlueStone sees negligible exposure, with LGDs under 1% of revenue since most customers buy lower-ticket everyday items rather than large solitaires. 

PNGS Reva is similarly protected — 97% of their products use star-melee diamonds, where the price gap between natural and lab-grown is only 10-15%, far too small to meaningfully shift buying behavior.

The unit economics driving each company's margin story

-->BlueStone's operating leverage engine — Pre-Ind AS EBITDA expanded 134.6% YoY to ₹54.8 Cr, while marketing spend stayed disciplined at 6.9% of revenue. 

There's also a genuine structural tailwind coming: 

non-cash ESOP charges, heavily front-loaded at ₹92.7 Cr in FY26, are guided to taper to ₹57.5 Cr in FY27E and drop a full 95% to just ₹4.8 Cr by FY30E — an automatic, built-in boost to reported PAT over the coming years as that expense simply fades away. Mature store cohorts are compounding at 30%+ SSSG, with store-level ROICs approaching 40%.

-->PNGS Reva's asset-light efficiency — the 28.8% EBITDA margin comes largely from the zero-rent, low-overhead nature of the Shop-in-Shop model operating inside existing PNGS mother stores, where total operating expenses were just 7% of revenue in Q1 FY27. 

Annualized inventory turnover stood at 1.29x, right in line with premium diamond retail benchmarks of 0.75x-1.5x.

Network expansion — different speeds, different formats

-->BlueStone: added 12 net new stores in Q1 alone (+60 YoY), spread across Tier-1 (180 stores), Tier-2 (102), and Tier-3 (70) — genuine pan-India geographic diversification. Strategy going forward: ~20% annual store network growth, or roughly 70-80 new stores a year.

-->PNGS Reva: regionally concentrated for now, with Maharashtra alone housing 32 stores, alongside a presence in Gujarat and Karnataka. 

Using ₹286.6 Cr in net IPO proceeds, they're rolling out 15 new Company-Owned flagship stores (2 already live), with a break-even profile of just 12 months for Maharashtra COCOs and 15-18 months for stores outside the state.

Where each company is headed next

-->BlueStone's vision — targeting ₹12,000 Cr in revenue within 4 years, implying roughly a 50% revenue CAGR (30% from fundamental SSSG, 20% from store additions). 

Operating EBITDA margins are guided to expand from today's 7.5% toward 15.0% as corporate scale kicks in and ESOP costs taper off. Blended inventory turns are targeted to accelerate to 1.7-1.8x.

-->PNGS Reva's roadmap — deploying those 15 new COCO boutiques across Tier-1 and metro markets, launching a proprietary D2C e-commerce website by August 2026, and guiding full-year sustainable EBITDA at 25-27% with PAT margins at 22-23% (factoring in typically higher H2 marketing spend around the festive season). 

EBO (company-owned store) sales share is expected to rise to 20-25% of revenue within 3 years, up from a much smaller base today.

How I'd score this head-to-head, pillar by pillar

-->Scale and geographic reach: BlueStone — 352 stores across 139 cities and a ₹733 Cr quarterly run rate give it genuine pan-India diversification that Reva's more Western-concentrated footprint doesn't yet match.

-->Unit profitability and margins: PNGS Reva — 28.8% EBITDA and 23.1% PAT margins lead the entire retail sector, enabled directly by the asset-light Shop-in-Shop cost structure.

-->SSSG and growth momentum: PNGS Reva — 119.5% YoY revenue growth and ~50% SIS same-store growth outpaced the category, helped by the festive Akshaya Tritiya quarter tailwind.

-->Digital tech and in-house moat: BlueStone — an in-house integrated tech stack, 80%+ digital discovery before purchase, and 95%+ in-house manufacturing genuinely prevent design IP leakage to competitors.

-->Balance sheet and cash reserves: PNGS Reva — ₹324 Cr in cash and equivalents post-IPO, with a fully debt-free roadmap for all their planned COCO showroom expansions.

Why I'm sharing this

Neither is a clean "better" pick — they're solving the same consumer shift with fundamentally different capital structures. 

BlueStone is the larger, tech-driven scale play still working its way toward retail-grade margins, with a real structural tailwind coming as ESOP costs fade. 

PNGS Reva is the smaller, already highly profitable heritage-backed operator, proving out its low-capex expansion model before scaling harder. Both are worth tracking, for very different reasons.

Urabn company's Indian growth rate has been accelerating recently. 

What it does?

Urban Company is a managed marketplace for home and beauty services i.e. cleaning, salon-at-home, appliance repair, plumbing, electricals, pest control. The distinction that matters is "managed": it isn't a listings board. 

The platform controls discovery, scheduling, pricing, professional assignment, payment, tracking, reviews and support, and invests in training and verification of the professionals rather than just generating leads. 

It monetises mainly through a commission on completed jobs, typically in the 20–30% range depending on category and city. Oye LabsClarro
It now runs four business lines:

1. India consumer services which is the profitable core. In Q1 FY27, excluding InstaHelp, NTV grew 29% YoY to ₹1,056 crore with adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 6.9% of NTV from 5.2%. 

2. InstaHelp which is quick-service housekeeping, the big investment bet, which crossed 100,000 delivered orders in a single day on 2 August 2026 and carried an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹132 crore in the June quarter. 

3. Native which is their own-brand consumer durables (water purifiers, smart locks); FY26 revenue up 130% to ₹267 crore. 

4. International : UAE and Singapore are profitable; the Saudi JV is approaching profitability. 

Why it's a convenience play. Three layers, roughly in ascending order of how much convenience the customer is actually buying:

Trust and standardisation. The Indian home services market is informal. For eg- you find a plumber through your building's WhatsApp group and have no idea what it costs or whether he'll show up. UC's product is really the removal of search cost, price negotiation and verification risk. That's a convenience good masquerading as a services marketplace.

Time and location shifting. Salon-at-home is the clearest case: the same haircut, but you don't travel and don't wait. The customer is paying a premium for their own hours back.

Time compression. InstaHelp delivers cleaning, dishwashing, laundry and meal prep within 10–15 minutes of booking which is the quick-commerce logic applied to labour. Once the fulfilment window collapses to minutes, the purchase stops being a planned transaction and becomes an impulse, which is exactly what lifts order frequency: orders were up 79% YoY to 13.2 million in Q1 FY27.

So, what drove the huge jump in spreads?

Gandhar’s gross spread jumped from ₹8,274/kL to ₹28,145/kL.

Q1 saw Middle East disruptions, delayed Saudi supplies and uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz.

Gandhar responded by:

→ Supplementing Saudi supplies with South Korean + Indian sourcing
→ Maintaining around 30–40 days of raw-material inventory
→ Buying at the right time and price
→ Keeping customer supplies uninterrupted

That last part mattered.
Gandhar was able to take price increases across categories, supporting higher realisations and spreads.

Management also said inventory gains were not the primary driver - the bigger benefit came from selling at higher prices.

BEHARI LAL ENGINEERING | HIGH-VALUE PRODUCT SHIFT

Business Profile
- B2B precision-engineering manufacturer of customised alloy steel products.
- Product portfolio includes metal rolls, engineering castings and forged products.
- FY26 revenue stood at ~₹534 Cr.
- Alloy steel contributed ~46% of revenue.
- Metal rolls contributed ~26%.
- Engineering castings contributed ~20%.

Manufacturing Strength
- Integrated setup covering melting, casting, rolling, machining and testing.
- Common infrastructure supports multiple product categories.
- Capacity utilisation reached ~88% in FY26.
- Integrated capabilities support customised product manufacturing.

Customer Stickiness
- Customer base exceeded 1,825 in FY26.
- ~84.7% of revenue came from repeat customers.
- Top 10 customers have an average relationship of ~6 years.
- Customised products require qualification, testing, audits and approvals.
- These processes create switching friction for customers.
- Top 10 customers contributed ~38% of FY26 revenue.

High-Value Product Shift
- High-value products contributed ~57.8% of FY26 revenue.
- Contribution increased from ~45.5% in FY25.
- Shift towards specialised products could improve business economics.
- Company reportedly met ~10% of India's metal-roll demand in FY24.

Moat & Risks
- Potential moat lies in customer qualifications and manufacturing know-how.
- Integrated capabilities and customer relationships add further stickiness.
- No long-term contracts with customers.
- Business remains exposed to competition and imports.
- Raw-material prices and customer concentration remain key risks.
- Not yet a wide-moat business.

Key Takeaway
- Behari Lal is gradually moving towards higher-value engineered products.
- Strong repeat business indicates meaningful customer stickiness.
- Future value creation depends on premium product mix and export growth.
- Improving returns on incremental capital will be crucial.
- Current view: PASS, but business remains on the tracking list.

JPM on Dixon Tech
OW, TP Rs 16400

Government launched Mobile phone manufacturing scheme (MPMS) with an outlay of Rs625bn

How can it play out for Dixon:
1) There is an eligibility criteria of Rs100bn turnover in FY26 for mobile phone manufacturers, including EMS companies, meaning the benefit may not apply to all of Dixon’s customers, thereby limiting benefits only to top customers.
2) There is a sales threshold of Rs50bn required over FY26 sales to avail incentives, meaning the scheme seems to be focused more on exports given domestic mobile shipments seem to have hit a ceiling for the industry; hence, for Dixon to avail benefits it will have to ramp up exports.
3) There is a 1.5% additional incentive on local sourcing of components and sub-assemblies, where Dixon should be eligible to get incentives of 0.6% given it is scaling up manufacturing of camera modules and display modules.

While all these factors should lead to earnings upgrades, quantum of that is still unclear as it will be dependent on
1) export volumes Dixon can achieve over the scheme period,
2) negotiations with brands on incentive sharing.

High reliance on the impacted German automotive sector and high client concentration pose downside risks.

Maintaining business continuity with Volkswagen will be a critical monitorable.

UPL is maintaining tight control over inventories in Latin America amid El Niño risks.

Marketing for the Advanta IPO is expected to begin soon.

Nomura expects the Oriental Hotels acquisition to be EPS accretive for Indian Hotels.

Further cost synergies could provide additional earnings benefits.

Asset optimisation and property upgrades could drive EBITDA higher.

The merger will also simplify the group’s holding structure.

HSBC ON INDIA STRATEGY — NEUTRAL

HSBC says Indian corporate earnings remain resilient for now despite the oil shock.

Results have come in ahead of expectations, with small & mid-cap earnings growth standing out.

GST cuts and RBI easing supported demand, while price hikes and inventory gains helped offset higher raw-material costs.

HSBC sees FY27 earnings growth at 14.3%, but expects some of the current support to fade in H2.

Maintains a Neutral stance on India within Asia.

Elevated commodity prices pose a risk of earnings downgrades in coming quarters.

🏦 US Treasury’s expansion of buybacks of long-dated government debt has revived the “debasement trade” that helped drive gold’s strong 2025 rally.

💵 Concerns over rising US debt, persistent inflation and dollar weakness are strengthening demand for gold as an alternative store of value.

📊 Gold-backed ETFs have recorded increased inflows in recent weeks, indicating broader investor participation and stronger investment demand.

**MORGAN STANLEY ON VISHAL MEGA MART — OVERWEIGHT | TP ₹146**

Morgan Stanley sees the 5-year reappointment of the MD & CEO as a key positive.

The move reduces uncertainty around management succession, which had been a key overhang.

It could help ease market concerns around leadership continuity.

The stock has corrected 14% over the past three months.

Morgan Stanley believes Vishal Mega Mart trades relatively cheap versus discretionary peers despite its consistent execution.

JEFFERIES ON POWER SECTOR

Jefferies expects the private power sector to grow faster than PSUs, with higher earnings CAGR over the next decade.

Around 63% of India’s incremental power capacity addition during FY26–30E is expected to come from private players, largely driven by renewables.

India’s power demand is estimated to grow at ~6% CAGR over FY26–30E.

Private-sector power generation is expected to grow faster at ~9% CAGR.

Jefferies remains constructive on the power sector, with Adani Energy Solutions and JSW Energy as its top private-sector picks.

MACQUARIE ON MONSOONS

Macquarie sees the current situation as a rainfall delay rather than crop distress, though close monitoring remains necessary.

Sowing activity is catching up, while healthy reservoir levels are cushioning the rainfall deficit.

Reservoir storage remains healthy across much of India, providing support to agriculture.

Food-supply and inflation risks have moderated since June.

However, the remaining rainfall deficit means crop yields will depend on the distribution of late-season rains

KOTAK SECURITIES ON MOBILE PHONE MANUFACTURING SCHEME

The new scheme introduces a two-track framework for mobile manufacturing.

Target Scheme 1 focuses on scaling manufacturing and localisation, with a demanding 15% moving-baseline revenue growth target.

Target Scheme 2 aims to promote and strengthen Indian smartphone brands.

Kotak believes exports will be critical to consistently meet growth hurdles, given largely flat domestic smartphone sales.

India’s mobile production growth has been predominantly export-led.

For Dixon Technologies, the scheme could provide a 14–22 bps EBITDA margin uplift.
